newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Constraints seen in Thai baht controls.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Constraints seen in Thai baht controls.

text.p: Singapore-style currency controls contemplated by the Bank of Thailand for the baht are expected to bring much-needed stability to the embattled currency, analysts said on Friday.
But questions remain about how such controls would be applied to gain best benefits for Thailand which faces several constraints that Singapore does not have, they told Reuters.
Thai authorities have said they are thinking of the possibility of using Singapore-style controls as a model for a revamped baht exchange rate system.

The Thai authorities' plans came after speculative attacks on the baht and the launch of central bank measures to curb baht supply from local sources to foreign speculators. The Bank of Thailand is determined to institutionalise these controls soon.

Analysts cautioned that the currency systems of Thailand and Singapore were quite different. Singapore has a free-floating system while Thailand pegs its baht to a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar.

The Thai unit's peg to the basket makes it a stable currency but also an easy prey for currency predators. Moreover, Singapore is an exporter of capital while Thailand is a net importer of funds which force its central bank to be defensive about its currency, analysts said.

Singapore's currency has no fixed band within which it must be traded but Thailand's central bank fixes a midrate daily for the baht against the dollar. The central bank allows a fluctuation of up to two satangs up or down when it trades dollars with local banks.

Analysts said Singapore discreetly manages its forex policy on a quarterly basis, setting some sort of informal targets for the currency's performance over the period. If its unit deviates from the desired target, the authorities signal displeasure to the market as a way to influence the foreign exchange level.
The Singapore government also restricts any loans to offshore parties of more than S$5.0 million. These loans must be approved by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

The Bank of Thailand's latest currency controls were aimed at curbing speculative attacks on the baht as these intermittent forays have been painful to handle for the central bank since it liberalised the forex market in 1991.

"The baht should not be an offshore currency in the first place. It was a mistake that we rushed to liberalise the financial system ahead of our ability to handle the situation," said a top Thai financial official who asked not to be named.

The sporadic attacks drained the central bank resources and left it with very little room to manage monetary policy, forcing it to maintain high interest rates to protect the baht, even at times of economic slumps as the one ongoing now.

Since mid-May, when the latest central bank controls were launched, a two-tier baht market with one offshore and the other onshore has developed. Speculators have been punished by the controls and those in need of baht to cover short positions were forced to acquire it at exorbitant costs abroad.

They are now guessing in which direction the Bank of Thailand is heading. But despite the ongoing confusion, some still believe any refinement along the lines of the Singapore model will be more effective than controls currently imposed.

"This (Singapore model) will be seen as a workable replacement for a blanket ban on baht outflow to the offshore market which is currently in place in Thailand," said an analyst at the Singapore-based research house I.D.E.A.

"The present system, as indicated perhaps by the continued falloff on the local stock market and the tightness of the interbank market is far from sustainable, and its operation threatens more economic relocation," he added.
But Chia Woon Khian, head of Asian research at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken, believed the Singapore model could not be effective for Thailand if its currency system was not modified.

"If you want to follow the Singapore model, you have to follow it to the fullest extent. You cannot have a cake and eat it at the same time," she said. "The Thai baht is stuck to the peg...and so there is no free market prices mechanism at work here. You will end up segregating the two markets."

The two-tier market normally tended to induce certain degrees of hestitation from investors and could affect capital inflows, not only hot money but also much-needed trade and investment-linked capital, said ING Barings head of research, Varut Siwasariyanon.
"With the present economic situation, it is not easy to make investors confident in Thailand," he said.
